concept.name: Cross-sectional momentum
concept.definition: The anomaly and strategy class of buying securities with the highest recent returns relative to their peers and selling those with the lowest, over 3- to 12-month formation and holding periods. Jegadeesh and Titman (1993) documented that such relative-strength portfolios generated significant abnormal returns not explained by systematic risk or delayed reaction to common factors.
concept.intuition: Winners keep winning and losers keep losing for a while: rank the whole market by recent performance, buy the top decile, short the bottom, and let the persistence work over the next quarter.
concept.mechanics: Each month, rank stocks by past J-month return (J = 3-12), form decile portfolios, buy the top decile and short the bottom, and hold for K months (K = 3-12) with overlapping monthly cohorts. Jegadeesh-Titman found the strongest strategies earning roughly 1% per month in 1965-1989 data, with part of the first-year abnormal return dissipating over the following two years.
concept.formula: Momentum return = R(top decile by past J-month return) - R(bottom decile), measured over holding period K and averaged across overlapping (J,K) cohorts.
concept.failure_modes: Momentum crashes - violent reversals concentrated in rebound phases after market declines - can erase years of gains in months, and turnover plus short-side costs are large; the published anomaly has decayed as it became crowded.
concept.misconceptions: That it is a free lunch refuting market efficiency; subsequent literature ties the premium to crash risk, behavioral underreaction, and trading costs - it is a risky, capacity-constrained anomaly, not an arbitrage.
concept.example: Rank 3,000 stocks by trailing 6-month return, buy the top 300 and short the bottom 300, hold 3 months, and reform monthly; Jegadeesh-Titman's tests show the best such zero-cost portfolios averaging about 1% per month before costs.

citations.source: Jegadeesh & Titman, 'Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers: Implications for Stock Market Efficiency', Journal of Finance 48(1), 1993, 65-91 (EconPapers record)
